en: The Inquiry of Nārāyaṇa: The Noble Dhāraṇī of the Great Illusion, the Victorious One.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling on the peak of Mount Suvarṇaśṛṅga in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa.

There, he was teaching a Dharma discourse called "The Gateway to the Light of Dharma," which had been praised by many beings, including gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, vidyādharas, and apsarases.

Then Nārāyaṇa—seized, cast out, defeated, and deprived of his splendor by the asuras—approached the Blessed One; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
He stands firm. ||1||
Standing to one side, Nārāyaṇa made this request:

"May the Blessed One—the omniscient, the all-seeing, who is compassionate toward all sentient beings—teach that Dharma-discourse which these gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others, or human beings, by upholding it, shall become victorious in battle, or against the falling of great spears, or against all calamities, or against all discursive thoughts and deliberations. ||2||
The Blessed One said: "O Nārāyaṇa, you are a master of illusion;
you possess illusion and are of great power. You deceive sentient beings with a manifold net of illusions."
Why do you ask this question regarding victory in battle out of fear? ||3||
Nārāyaṇa spoke thus:
"O Blessed One, here I have been conquered by the illusory power of Kāmāsura, the lord of the asuras.
Some of the gods have died, some have fled, and some have been destroyed."
Therefore, O Blessed One, teach that Dharma discourse by which these beings shall be victors in battle;
the asuras shall be defeated, their pride diminished, and they shall be overcome. ||4||
The Blessed One said:
"In the past, in a time long gone, on Mount Rohita in Magadha, there was a king named Ratnaśrī.

At that time and at that moment, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata named Sarveśvara—an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed."
The Blessed One, the Buddha, the teacher of gods and men, came into existence. ||5||

From the presence of that Blessed One, the Lord of All, I have well-grasped, retained, recited, understood, and rejoiced in these mantra-words of knowledge named *Mahāmāyāvijayavāhinī*, and they have been revealed in detail by me to others. By the power of this dhāraṇī, O Nārāyaṇa, there shall never be fear of enemies, fear of the unwholesome, or fear of thieves.

Having ruled the kingdom righteously for hundreds of thousands of years, he subsequently traveled from city to city in happiness, as if on a pleasure excursion through a grove, by the power of the *dhāraṇī*. In another birth, the Bodhisattva became a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) named Māndhātṛ,
endowed with the seven jewels.
He promulgated his command throughout the ends of the three worlds.
Previously, through the perfection of the virtue of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), he rained down wealth according to the desires of all beings for their benefit and happiness;
thus, he became the bringer of happiness and the benefactor of all beings.
Namely, by the power of the *nārāyaṇāsya* dhāraṇī, he brought the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) to fulfillment over many hundreds of thousands of eons.
Furthermore, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, vidyādharas, humans, and non-humans who dwell in their respective directions did not turn away from him.

Having spent sixty-four thousand eons previously, he was later liberated from the fear of garuḍas in a single lifetime; established like a lord of nāgas, he became the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One.
For he was the unsurpassed Arhat in the world, the teacher of the gods. ||6||
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa, you should take up these mantra syllables of the dhāraṇī named *Mahāmāyāvijayavāhinī*.
They are as follows: Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas established throughout the paths; homage to all mudrās and mantra syllables.

Oṃ māye mahāmāye mahāmāyādhāraṇi! This is she, by means of the mantra of Mahāmāyā and in the form of Mahāmāyā: whirl, whirl those beings who contemplate Virūḍhaka; all those wicked beings, cause them to whirl, cause them to whirl; delude, delude; cause them to faint, cause them to faint;
slay, slay; destroy, destroy!

Kill, kill, O Great Illusion! Alala-lale! O you whose face is the thousandfold net of great illusion, with a thousand heads, a thousand arms, and blazing eyes; O you who contain within your heart the essence of all Tathāgatas; O you who hold in your hands swords, bows, axes, nooses, *tomaras*, spears, and severed human heads; O you who hold mallets and wheels in your hands! Come, come, Blessed Lady! By the truth of all Tathāgatas, by the truth of the hosts of divine sages, O bearer of the victorious Great Illusion! Remember, remember! Go forth in the form of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas!
Go, O destroyer of all obscurations, O disperser of enemy armies! Delude, delude all the wicked ones, both myself and all sentient beings!
Protect, protect me and all sentient beings from the terrors and calamities of yakṣas! Svāhā!
Om, to the dhāraṇī of Mahāmāyā, svāhā!
Oṃ, empowered by the great maṇḍala, svāhā!
Oṃ, to her who is saluted and worshipped by the Vajra-holder, svāhā!
Oṃ, to the beloved of Padmapāṇi, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to her who is saluted by all the gods, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to her who is praised and worshipped by the host of Mothers, svāhā!
Oṃ, victory! svāhā!
[Oṃ vijaye svāhā | oṃ svāhā | oṃ avidhite svāhā |]
Oṃ aparājite svāhā | Oṃ mohanīye svāhā | Oṃ stambhanāye svāhā |
Oṃ jambhanīye svāhā | Oṃ jayantiye svāhā | Oṃ bhramaṇīye svāhā |
Oṃ bhramaṇīye svāhā! Oṃ sarvāsuradamanīye svāhā! Oṃ mahākālavanditapūjitāyai svāhā!
Oṃ kāmarūpiṇīye svāhā | Oṃ māyārākṣasīye svāhā | Oṃ rara svāhā |
Oṃ rū rū hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ he he jaye māyā bhagavati mahāmāyāvijayavāhinī gṛhāṇa | śīghram āvilambasva mama sarvasattvānāṃ ca sarvakāryaṃ kuru kuru hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā ||7||
Nārāyaṇa, you yourself should take up these secret mantra-words called *Mahāmāyāvijayavāhinī* and recite them, and then teach them extensively to the other [side].
Nārāyaṇa, furthermore, in that final conflict between the two armies, one should place this *dhāraṇī*-wheel in five locations upon the representation of a chariot.

Nārāyaṇa, in the midst of both [armies], at the front of the enemy army, within that chariot, one should install the Queen of Vidyās named *Mahāmāyāvijayavāhinī*, who has many hundreds of thousands of forms, many hundreds of thousands of arms, and three eyes.
One should visualize her as red and black in color, with four blazing faces, appearing as if she were devouring the enemy army.

Having himself assumed the form of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), and having written the *dhāraṇī* with saffron at midday, the king, obscuring the enemy's army with his own nature which is like an illusion, will become victorious through various essential means.
Nārāyaṇa, I declare that these noble warriors have been conquered and defeated; some have fainted and are falling to the ground.
Nārāyaṇa, having fallen thus due to their ten unwholesome deeds, they are carried away because the path has been cut off.
And for them, life does not bear its intended fruit.
Nārāyaṇa, such is the power of this praised dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa, for some these mantra-words of the dhāraṇī may be suitable through purity or impurity;
they may be suitable whether by fasting or without fasting.

One should recite it three times every day. By that alone, having exhausted even an accumulation of the five sins of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), one attains a mass of merit, becomes a rememberer of past lives (*jātismara*),
becomes an enjoyer of all-pervading wealth among all sentient beings, delights in wholesome dharmas, and does not engage in unwholesome, perverse, or sinful acts.

Furthermore, O Nārāyaṇas, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family, monk or nun, layman or laywoman, king or prince, brahmin, or even a preacher of the True Dharma who has died and passed away while upholding this *dhāraṇī*, or who has been burned to ashes— if any man or woman should touch them, that person will certainly become one who remembers their past lives.

Then Nārāyaṇa, the protector of the Bodhisattvas, thinking, "Oh, how wonderful!", rose from his seat, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, flowers, and garlands; having circumambulated the Blessed One three times and prostrated before him, with a smiling face, he praised the Blessed One with this verse:
"Oh! Among the worlds of asuras and gods, you are the eldest and the most excellent, truly unsurpassed."
O Śiva, peaceful, ungraspable, and transcending the world—salutations be unto you!
The non-existence of all phenomena reveals the true nature of phenomena;
you who are liberated from both merit and demerit, O Dharma, Truth, homage be to you! (8)
Then Nārāyaṇa, having bowed to the Blessed One and thinking, "O Blessed One, you are my sovereign," departed.

The Blessed One, being well-pleased, spoke these words; and those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, vidyādharas, apsarases, and so forth, as well as that entire assembly and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One. Thus ends the ninth [chapter].
The *Nārāyaṇaparipṛcchā*, the Noble Dhāraṇī called the *Mahāmāyāvijayavāhinī*, is completed.
